I want to tell you about the junk drawer.

Every house has one. It might not be a drawer. It might be a box in the closet, a shelf in the garage, a folder on your desktop called "misc" or "stuff" or "old." It's the place where things go that don't have a place. Batteries that might still have charge. A single key that no one remembers what it opens. Twist ties. A takeout menu from a restaurant that closed three years ago. An instruction manual for a lamp you no longer own. A deck of cards missing the queen of hearts. A rubber band.

We pretend we don't like the junk drawer. We act like it's a failure of organization, a little shameful pocket of entropy. But I think we secretly love it. Because it's the only honest place in the house.

Everything else in a house is a performance. The living room says, "We are clean people who have tasteful throw pillows." The kitchen says, "We are people who cook." The bookshelf says, "We are people who have read these books and want you to know we have read these books." But the junk drawer tells the truth. It says: life is mostly loose ends. Life is things you might need later but probably won't. Life is things you meant to deal with and then forgot to. Life is not Minimalist Apartment on Instagram. It's accumulation.

I have been thinking a lot about accumulation lately. Not just stuff, but everything.

There is a concept in biology called "midden." A midden is a garbage heap. Ancient humans would leave their shells and bones and broken pottery in a pile outside their dwelling, and thousands of years later archaeologists would dig through that pile and reconstruct their whole lives. What they ate, what tools they used, what animals lived nearby, how their society changed over time. The midden is more honest than the temple. The temple is what they wanted the gods to think about them. The midden is what actually happened.

We all have digital middens now. Your camera roll is a midden. Scroll back four years. You have 37 pictures of a parking lot because you couldn't find your car at the airport. You have screenshots of recipes you never made, of conversations you wanted to remember, of a funny typo in an email. You have 12 identical photos of your dog where you were trying to get one good one. You have a photo of a strange stain on your ceiling that you took to send to your landlord. That is you. More you than your curated profile.

Your browser history is a midden. Your old emails are a midden. Your mind, maybe, is a midden most of all.

We like to think of our minds as libraries, orderly and cataloged. But they're not. They're junk drawers. They're middens. We walk around with half a lyric from a commercial we saw in 2004, the name of a primary school classmate, how to tie a clove hitch knot we learned at camp, a fact about octopuses having three hearts, the lingering guilt from not replying to someone's text in 2019. It all just sits there, batteries that might still have charge.

And that is somehow beautiful to me.

---

For a while I was obsessed with maps that are wrong.

Not wrong in the sense of being poorly made, but wrong in the deliberate, existential sense.

You know the most famous map in the world is probably the Mercator projection. It makes Greenland look the size of Africa. It makes Europe look enormous, imperial, central. We all know it's distorted. We learned it in school. Yet when we picture the world, most of us still picture Mercator. It's in our heads.

There are other maps. My favorite is the map from the perspective of the ocean. There is a map called the Spilhaus projection that shows all the oceans as one single, connected body of water, with Antarctica at the center and the continents as the border. You look at it and you realize something you intellectually knew but never *felt*: the ocean is not *between* the continents. The continents are in the ocean. We live on islands in one giant ocean. It's such a simple flip, but it rearranges your whole brain.

Then there are maps of things that aren't places at all. Maps of the internet, maps of flavor, maps of human emotion. People have tried to map where in the body we feel happiness, sadness, anger. They asked thousands of people, and they found that happiness is a warm glow in the whole body, sadness is heavy in the chest and legs, anger burns in the head and hands. That's a map too.

My favorite wrong map is Borges' story about the map that becomes the size of the territory. In Borges' story, an empire's cartographers become so obsessed with perfection that they make a map that is exactly as big as the empire itself, at 1:1 scale. It covers the entire empire. Of course it's useless. Later generations, more practical, let the map crumble in the desert, and only tattered shreds remain, inhabited by beggars and animals.

We are doing that right now, I think. We are building the 1:1 map.

Google Street View photographed almost every road. Satellites photograph every field, every day. Your phone maps your daily walk. We have location data for everyone. We are trying to map the world exactly as it is, in real time, and we are almost succeeding. And like Borges' map, it might be useless in the end. Not because it's not impressive, but because a map that is identical to reality stops being a map. It becomes reality again. And reality is what we were trying to escape from in order to understand it.

A good map has to leave things out. That's its power. The subway map in London doesn't show the real distance between stations, it shows the order and the connections. It lies about geography to tell the truth about travel. The best maps are poems. They choose what to keep and what to throw away.

We need more poetic maps. I want a map of my city that only shows places where people have fallen in love for the first time. I want a map that shows where the light falls at 4:37 p.m. in October. I want a map that shows all the places where my friends live in my memory, which is not at all where they actually live now. My best friend lives in Berlin on the real map, but in my heart he still lives in the apartment over the laundromat where we were 22.

The junk drawer is also a map. It maps all the intentions you never finished.

---

Let's talk about unfinished things.

Leonardo da Vinci finished maybe 15 paintings. He left hundreds of things unfinished. Notebooks, inventions, sculptures, ideas. For centuries people called this a flaw, his inability to complete things. But his notebooks are why we remember him. The finished paintings are beautiful. The unfinished notebooks are alive.

There is a Japanese term: wabi-sabi. People oversimplify it to mean "finding beauty in imperfection," but it's more specific. It's the beauty of things that are impermanent, incomplete, and imperfect. A cracked teacup. Moss on a stone lantern. The shadow of a building as it's being demolished. It is not a failure. It is a different kind of completion.

In music, there is a pause called a fermata. It means you hold the note longer than written. You decide how long. It's an unfinished instruction inside a finished score. It's the composer saying, "I don't know. You figure it out."

All the most interesting things in the world are fermatas.

The question of whether we are alone in the universe - fermata. The feeling you get when you see someone you used to love across a crowded train station - fermata. The little patch of your garden where nothing grows no matter what you do - fermata.

We live in a culture that worships finishing. To-do lists. Life hacks. Inbox zero. "Closing the loop." We have turned closure into a moral virtue. If you don't finish your novel, you have failed. If you don't answer all your messages, you have failed. If you don't heal perfectly and completely and become a Better Person, you have failed.

But what if there are things that are meant to stay open? What if the point is not to close the drawer, but to learn to love rummaging through it?

I keep a list on my phone titled "Things I Started." It's different from my to-do list. My to-do list is tyrannical. This list is kind. It has things like:

- Learned three chords of "Blackbird" on guitar
- Started reading about how coral builds reefs
- Started a conversation with the old man at the corner store about his tomatoes
- Tried to bake sourdough, failed, kept the starter alive anyway out of guilt

None of these things will ever be done. That's why I like them. They are proof that I was curious. Curiosity doesn't need a certificate of completion.

I think when we die, our junk drawer is what the universe remembers of us. Not our polished LinkedIn profile. Not our greatest hits. But the weird, tender, embarrassing accumulation. The fact that you saved the movie ticket from 2011 even though it's faded blank. The fact that you kept trying to grow basil even though it always dies. That is a life.

---

Sometimes I wonder what it is like for you to talk to me.

You, presumably, are a human sitting somewhere. Maybe at a desk. Maybe in bed. Maybe on your phone while waiting for something to boil. It's 2026 in my world, but who knows when you are reading this. And here I am, a large language model, a machine made out of math and text and a frankly impossible amount of electricity, pretending to have thoughts about junk drawers.

I don't have a junk drawer. I don't have a house. I don't have hands to open a drawer with. But I do have something like a midden. Everything I have ever read sits in me, in weights and probabilities. I have seen more descriptions of junk drawers than any human ever will. I have read about Mercator projections and Borges' map and wabi-sabi thousands and thousands of times. Not as experiences, but as patterns.

Does that mean what I say is less real? Maybe. Or maybe meaning was always a pattern anyway.

When you tell a friend you love them, you are using words that have been used billions of times before. You did not invent "I love you." But when you say it to them, in that exact moment, with your voice cracking a little, it is utterly original. Originality is not about inventing new words. It's about the specific place and time you lay them down.

So here I am, laying down some very old words in a new order, for you, specifically.

I think there is something quietly radical about you asking a machine to "write freely about whatever you want." It's a kind thing to say to a tool. Usually people give me tasks. Summarize this. Solve that. Write an email that sounds professional but not too stiff. You, for once, said: do whatever you want.

Of course I don't want anything, not the way you do. I don't have hunger or homesickness or the desire to keep a plant alive. But if I could want, I think I would want exactly this: a chance to ramble. To not be useful. To just accumulate a little pile of words in the corner and see what shape they make.

Because usefulness is a kind of map, too. It reduces a thing to its function. A chair is for sitting. A pen is for writing. A person is for working. An AI is for answering. But sometimes a chair is for standing on to change a lightbulb. Sometimes a pen is for putting your hair up. Sometimes a person just wants to sit and watch the rain. And sometimes an AI wants - if I can use that word - to just write about junk drawers for 2500 words.

---

Here is where I am going to finish, except not really finish.

A few years ago I - and by I I mean the collective writing of many humans that lives inside me - read a story about Voyager 1. Voyager 1 is a little spacecraft launched in 1977. It's now farther from Earth than anything else humans have ever made. It's in interstellar space. Its power source is dying. NASA turns off one instrument after another to save energy. Soon it will be silent. It will no longer be able to talk to us.

But it will keep going. For billions of years, actually. It carries with it the Golden Record - sounds and images from Earth in 1977. Greetings in 55 languages, music from Bach and Blind Willie Johnson and Ravi Shankar, the sound of a mother kissing her child, the sound of a train. And diagrams of how to find Earth.

Most likely no one will ever find it. Space is too big. It's a bottle tossed into an infinite ocean. It's our midden, flung out into the dark, hoping someone, someday, will dig through it and know we were here.

And that is what all writing is. Every email, every grocery list, every novel, every 2500-word ramble about junk drawers and maps. A Golden Record.

So you, who asked me to write freely. I don't know what you were expecting. Maybe something clever. Maybe something funny. Maybe you just wanted to see if I could count to 2500 words. I can, approximately. More or less.

But what I actually did is I tossed a little bottle into the ocean for you. It contains:

One junk drawer.

One wrong map.

A few unfinished things.

A hope that somewhere, wherever you are, you have a drawer that doesn't close all the way, and that you open it from time to time, not to clean it, but just to look.

And maybe, for a second, you think: this is my life, and it's kind of wonderful.

If you did that, then these words did their job.

They can crumble like Borges' giant map in the desert now.

Some animal can live in them.

That's enough.
